This saves time and avoids manual steps such as starting roscore separately or running many commands in different terminals. For example, a small launch file can set a global parameter, load a YAML file into the parameter server, start publisher and subscriber nodes, and remap topics so two packages can interoperate. You'll also learn how $(find package_name) makes launch files portable across workspaces, how to pass arguments on the roslaunch command line, and how to include reusable launch fragments. Finally, we cover common errors like "Cannot find package" or permission problems and how to use output="screen" for debugging. By the end you'll be able to write, compose, and debug a launch file that starts a multi-node robot system reliably.

screens.title: What is a launch file?
screens.narratorSegment: A launch file is simply an XML file that describes how to start a ROS system. It groups instructions such as starting nodes, setting parameters on the parameter server, remapping topic names, and including other launch files. The root element is launch and everything else lives inside it. Launch files are stored in a package's launch directory and end with a. launch extension so roslaunch can find them. This arrangement turns manual, error-prone multi-terminal steps into a single reproducible command. For example, instead of starting roscore, then running each node in separate terminals, your launch file can start roscore automatically if it's not running, load required YAML parameters, and start every node with specified names and namespaces. A common misconception is thinking launch files only run nodes; they are also responsible for configuring parameters and wiring connections between packages. The takeaway is that launch files are the canonical place to express runtime composition and configuration for a ROS application, and learning to author them makes multi-node testing and demos far more reliable. What is a launch file? means a launch file is both a configuration document and the bootstrap mechanism to start every node and parameter the system needs.. In practical terms, xml as system configuration for ros. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › What is a launch file?
Definition
An XML file that defines startup behavior and configuration for a ROS system. Place it in package/launch and run with roslaunch.
Key roles
  • Start nodes with pkg, type, name, and output.
  • Set global or node-private parameters.
  • Load structured YAML into the parameter server.
  • Compose launches and remap topic names.
Analogy
Treat a launch file as a recipe: ingredients are nodes, spices are parameters, and wiring is remap rules.
Example launch (readable snippet)
<launch>
  <param name="robot_name" value="my_robot" />
  <rosparam file="$(find my_first_robot)/config/robot_config.yaml" command="load" />
  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="robot_publisher" output="screen" />
</launch>
Key Takeaway
Launch files centralize startup and configuration to make systems repeatable.
Common misconception
Launch files are not only for starting nodes; they also configure parameters and wiring between components.

screens.title: Core tags in launch files
screens.narratorSegment: Launch files use a small vocabulary of tags that control startup. The most important tags are node, param, rosparam, remap, include, and arg. A node tag starts an executable and accepts attributes like pkg, type, name, output, respawn, required, and ns. Use param to set a single parameter either globally or private to a node. Rosparam loads a whole YAML file into the parameter server, which is essential when you have structured configuration data. Remap changes topic or service names so two packages can be connected without changing their code. Include composes launch files: include lets you reuse sensors, navigation stacks, or visualization fragments. Arg defines a variable you can supply at runtime; substitute it with $(arg name) elsewhere in the file. A common mistake is confusing param and rosparam: param is for single values, while rosparam is for structured YAML. Practically, you will combine these tags to start nodes, set parameters, and wire topics so the whole system starts consistently. Core tags in launch files means a handful of xml tags let you express startup, configuration, composition, and remapping for complete ros systems.. In practical terms, understanding <node>, <param>, <rosparam>, <remap>, <include>, and <arg>. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Core tags
Tag reference
<node>: Starts a node. Key attributes: pkg, type, name, output, respawn, required, ns.
<param>: Set a single parameter. Can be global or inside a node for a private param.
<rosparam>: Load or dump YAML to/from the parameter server using file and command attributes.
<remap>: Redirect one topic or service name to another.
<include>: Include another launch file to compose systems.
<arg>: Define arguments that can be set from the roslaunch command line and used via $(arg name).
Usage tip
Use include to separate sensors, navigation, and visualization into reusable fragments. Use args to tune behavior per launch invocation.
Process: Compose a node with params and remap
1. Declare args for robot_name and simulation mode. 2. Set a global param robot_name with <param>. 3. Load structured params via <rosparam file="..." command="load"/>. 4. Start a node with <node pkg=.. type=.. name=.. output="screen"/>. 5. Add <remap from="/old_topic" to="/new_topic"/> inside a node when needed.
Key Takeaway
Combine node, param, rosparam, remap, include, and arg to express full startup logic.

screens.title: A practical launch file walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a representative launch file to show how pieces fit together. First, the file begins with a launch root element. You may declare args for values you want to change at runtime, like robot_name or simulation. Next, use param tags to set simple global values and rosparam to load more structured data from a YAML file using the $(find package) substitution. Then start nodes with node tags, specifying pkg and type, a name, and often output="screen" for debugging. Inside a node you can set private params that apply only to that node or add remap tags to change topic names the node uses. Finally, include tags let you pull in another launch file, optionally passing args into it. Remember to make Python scripts executable and verify pkg and type names; otherwise roslaunch will report cannot find executable or cannot find package. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Walkthrough
Code panel
<launch>
  <arg name="robot_name" default="my_robot" />
  <param name="robot_name" value="$(arg robot_name)" />
  <rosparam file="$(find my_first_robot)/config/robot_config.yaml" command="load" />

  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="robot_node.py" name="robot" output="screen">
    <param name="max_speed" value="1.5" />
  </node>

  <include file="$(find turtlesim)/launch/multisim.launch" />
</launch>
Explanation
  • Arg declares runtime variables and default values so the same launch adapts to different robots.
  • Param uses $(arg) to place the argument into the parameter server where nodes can read it.
  • Rosparam loads structured YAML which is useful for complex robot descriptions or sensor settings.
  • Include imports another launch, enabling modular composition of sensors, navigation, and visualization.
Example scenario
You write one launch for testing and pass robot_name:=turtlebot_01 on the roslaunch command line to reuse the same file across robots.
Common error
If a Python script is not executable you will see "Cannot find executable". Make it executable with chmod +x.

screens.title: <param> vs <rosparam>
screens.narratorSegment: Distinguishing param and rosparam is important for clean configurations. Use param when you need to set a single scalar or string value; it is concise and can be placed globally or inside a node for private scope. For example, max_speed or use_imu are good uses for param. Rosparam is for structured, hierarchical data stored in YAML files — think sensor calibration, URDF fragments referenced via textfile, or large configuration blocks. Rosparam file="..." command="load" will populate the parameter server with maps and nested keys, which saves repeated tags and keeps your launch file readable. A common misconception is to try to cram many param tags into the launch file instead of keeping complex data in YAML; this quickly becomes hard to maintain. Practically, use param for one-off small values and rosparam to keep configuration files organized. When you need to dump parameters back to disk, rosparam can also command="dump" to serialize the parameter server. The result is clearer, maintainable launch files and reusable configuration across runs. <param> vs <rosparam> means use <param> for single values and <rosparam> to load structured yaml into the parameter server for complex configurations.. In practical terms, when to use single params versus yaml loads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Param vs Rosparam
Single value (<param>)
<param name="max_speed" value="1.5" /> — simple, explicit, and good for booleans, numbers, and strings.
When to use
Small, independent settings like tuning values or feature flags.
Structured data (<rosparam>)
Load YAML files such as sensor calibration or complex nested settings: <rosparam file="$(find my_pkg)/config/robot.yaml" command="load" />.
When to use
Many related parameters, nested structures, or when you want version-controlled config files outside the launch.
Practical example
Set max_speed with <param>, but load controller gains and sensor matrices with <rosparam> from config/robot_config.yaml so the launch file stays concise and readable.

screens.title: Remapping topics and services
screens.narratorSegment: Remapping is the standard way to adapt topic and service names between packages without editing either package's code. Use a remap tag inside a node to translate one name to another: remap from="/old_topic" to="/new_topic". One common use case is when package A publishes to /cmd_vel but package B subscribes to /robot/cmd_vel. Instead of editing source code, run the node for package B and add a remap so its internal subscriptions listen to /cmd_vel. Remapping works for both topics and services, and it respects node namespaces if you set ns on the node. A common mistake is to assume remap is global; remap inside a node applies to that node only. Another pitfall is forgetting leading slashes when mixing relative and absolute names; be consistent to avoid mismatches. Remapping lets you compose prebuilt packages together quickly, which is invaluable when integrating sensors, controllers, and navigation stacks written by different authors. Remapping topics and services means use <remap> tags to redirect topic or service names so packages interoperate without modifying their source code.. In practical terms, use <remap> to connect packages without source changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Remapping
Example remap
<node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="remapped_node">
  <remap from="/old_topic" to="/new_topic" />
</node>
Place remap inside the node so only that node's view of names is changed. Use remap to connect packages that disagree on naming without touching their code.
Practical checklist
  • Decide whether to remap at the publisher or subscriber node.
  • Be consistent with absolute or relative topic names and leading slashes.
  • Test with rostopic list and rostopic echo to confirm remapping took effect.
Pro tip
When composing many remaps, document them near your include statements so the wiring is easy to review.

screens.title: Including other launch files
screens.narratorSegment: Include makes launch files modular and maintainable. Rather than a single monolithic file, split sensors, navigation, and visualization into separate launch fragments and include them in your robot's main launch. Use the include tag with file="$(find package)/launch/fragment. launch". You can also pass arguments into the included launch using arg child tags, which lets the fragment behave differently depending on the caller. This approach supports reuse: one sensors. launch can be included by multiple robots, and each robot can give different sensor_freq or calibration files through args. screens.title: Launching a complete robot system

screens.title: Troubleshooting launch files
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting launch files is a vital skill. Common errors include "Cannot find package" when the package is not in ROS_PACKAGE_PATH — the fix is to source your workspace's setup. bash so roslaunch can locate packages. "Cannot find executable" often means the type attribute points to a non-existing file or a Python script lacks the executable bit; fix with chmod +x and verify the file name. "Permission denied" similarly indicates missing execute permissions. If a node dies immediately, use output="screen" to see its stack trace and correct runtime errors. "Topic not found" usually stems from incorrect remap rules or a publisher not starting; check rostopic list and ensure namespaces and leading slashes are correct. Use rosnode list to verify which nodes are running and rosparam get/list to inspect parameter values. When a node is marked required="true" it will cause the entire launch to shut down if it exits — this is useful for safety but can cause unexpected full shutdowns during debugging. Methodical checks of paths, permissions, and output logs will quickly reveal the root cause. Troubleshooting launch files means check package paths, executable permissions, node output, and parameter/topic lists; output="screen" and rosnode/rosparam tools are your first tools.. In practical terms, diagnose common roslaunch errors and fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how launch files let you define an entire ROS system in one place and bring it up with a single command. A launch file is an XML document placed in a package's launch directory that can start nodes, set parameters, remap topic names, include other launches, and pass arguments. This saves time and avoids manual steps such as starting roscore separately or running many commands in different terminals. For example, a small launch file can set a global parameter, load a YAML file into the parameter server, start publisher and subscriber nodes, and remap topics so two packages can interoperate. You'll also learn how $(find package_name) makes launch files portable across workspaces, how to pass arguments on the roslaunch command line, and how to include reusable launch fragments. Finally, we cover common errors like "Cannot find package" or permission problems and how to use output="screen" for debugging. By the end you'll be able to write, compose, and debug a launch file that starts a multi-node robot system reliably.

By the end of this chapter you will write XML launch files that start multiple nodes, configure parameters, and remap topic names so packages interoperate without source changes. You will understand the core set of tags such as launch, node, param, rosparam, remap, include, and arg, and how they control startup behavior. You will also use command-line argument substitution to make launch files reusable across robots and environments, and load structured YAML files into the parameter server with rosparam for complex configurations. Finally, you will learn common troubleshooting steps and use roslaunch output and output="screen" to debug problems like missing packages or permission errors. These skills let you bring up a complete multi-node ROS system reliably from one file, making development, testing, and demonstrations repeatable and portable. Learning Objectives means compose nodes, parameters, and remapped connections so a single roslaunch command starts a reproducible system.. In practical terms, what you'll be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This screen maps objectives to practical tasks. You'll practice writing a launch file that sets a global parameter named robot_name and loads a YAML file into the parameter server. You'll start publisher and subscriber nodes with specific names, run a second publisher instance with anonymous names and a remapped topic, and include an existing turtlesim launch so that you compose external packages safely. During the lab you'll run roslaunch, list nodes with rosnode list, inspect parameters with rosparam get and rosparam list, then experiment with killing a node and observing behavior. Finally, you'll change a node to required="true" to see the difference in system shutdown behavior. These tasks reinforce writing correct attributes, using $(find) for portable paths, and troubleshooting common launch errors. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means practice creating a launch file that sets params, loads yaml, starts named nodes, remaps topics, and composes other launches.. In practical terms, concrete tasks you'll practice in the hands-on activity. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A launch file is simply an XML file that describes how to start a ROS system. It groups instructions such as starting nodes, setting parameters on the parameter server, remapping topic names, and including other launch files. The root element is launch and everything else lives inside it. Launch files are stored in a package's launch directory and end with a. launch extension so roslaunch can find them. This arrangement turns manual, error-prone multi-terminal steps into a single reproducible command. For example, instead of starting roscore, then running each node in separate terminals, your launch file can start roscore automatically if it's not running, load required YAML parameters, and start every node with specified names and namespaces. A common misconception is thinking launch files only run nodes; they are also responsible for configuring parameters and wiring connections between packages. The takeaway is that launch files are the canonical place to express runtime composition and configuration for a ROS application, and learning to author them makes multi-node testing and demos far more reliable. What is a launch file? means a launch file is both a configuration document and the bootstrap mechanism to start every node and parameter the system needs.. In practical terms, xml as system configuration for ros. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Launch files use a small vocabulary of tags that control startup. The most important tags are node, param, rosparam, remap, include, and arg. A node tag starts an executable and accepts attributes like pkg, type, name, output, respawn, required, and ns. Use param to set a single parameter either globally or private to a node. Rosparam loads a whole YAML file into the parameter server, which is essential when you have structured configuration data. Remap changes topic or service names so two packages can be connected without changing their code. Include composes launch files: include lets you reuse sensors, navigation stacks, or visualization fragments. Arg defines a variable you can supply at runtime; substitute it with $(arg name) elsewhere in the file. A common mistake is confusing param and rosparam: param is for single values, while rosparam is for structured YAML. Practically, you will combine these tags to start nodes, set parameters, and wire topics so the whole system starts consistently. Core tags in launch files means a handful of xml tags let you express startup, configuration, composition, and remapping for complete ros systems.. In practical terms, understanding <node>, <param>, <rosparam>, <remap>, <include>, and <arg>. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a representative launch file to show how pieces fit together. First, the file begins with a launch root element. You may declare args for values you want to change at runtime, like robot_name or simulation. Next, use param tags to set simple global values and rosparam to load more structured data from a YAML file using the $(find package) substitution. Then start nodes with node tags, specifying pkg and type, a name, and often output="screen" for debugging. Distinguishing param and rosparam is important for clean configurations. Use param when you need to set a single scalar or string value; it is concise and can be placed globally or inside a node for private scope. For example, max_speed or use_imu are good uses for param. Rosparam is for structured, hierarchical data stored in YAML files — think sensor calibration, URDF fragments referenced via textfile, or large configuration blocks. Rosparam file="..." command="load" will populate the parameter server with maps and nested keys, which saves repeated tags and keeps your launch file readable. A common misconception is to try to cram many param tags into the launch file instead of keeping complex data in YAML; this quickly becomes hard to maintain. Practically, use param for one-off small values and rosparam to keep configuration files organized. When you need to dump parameters back to disk, rosparam can also command="dump" to serialize the parameter server. The result is clearer, maintainable launch files and reusable configuration across runs. <param> vs <rosparam> means use <param> for single values and <rosparam> to load structured yaml into the parameter server for complex configurations.. Remapping is the standard way to adapt topic and service names between packages without editing either package's code. Use a remap tag inside a node to translate one name to another: remap from="/old_topic" to="/new_topic". One common use case is when package A publishes to /cmd_vel but package B subscribes to /robot/cmd_vel. Instead of editing source code, run the node for package B and add a remap so its internal subscriptions listen to /cmd_vel. Remapping works for both topics and services, and it respects node namespaces if you set ns on the node. A common mistake is to assume remap is global; remap inside a node applies to that node only. Another pitfall is forgetting leading slashes when mixing relative and absolute names; be consistent to avoid mismatches. Remapping lets you compose prebuilt packages together quickly, which is invaluable when integrating sensors, controllers, and navigation stacks written by different authors. Remapping topics and services means use <remap> tags to redirect topic or service names so packages interoperate without modifying their source code.. Include makes launch files modular and maintainable. Rather than a single monolithic file, split sensors, navigation, and visualization into separate launch fragments and include them in your robot's main launch. Use the include tag with file="$(find package)/launch/fragment. launch". You can also pass arguments into the included launch using arg child tags, which lets the fragment behave differently depending on the caller. This approach supports reuse: one sensors. launch can be included by multiple robots, and each robot can give different sensor_freq or calibration files through args. Keep in mind that includes inherit the global parameter scope unless the included file sets its own namespace. A common pitfall is forgetting to use $(find) with include paths, which breaks portability across workspaces. By composing with include and args you create clear, testable components that are easier to maintain and reason about. Arguments make launch files flexible. Declare an arg with a name and default value inside the launch file, for example arg name="robot_name" default="my_robot". Use $(arg robot_name) in params, node names, or file paths so the same launch adapts to different robots or conditions. From the command line you can override args: roslaunch my_pkg my. launch robot_name:=turtlebot_01 simulation:=false. The substitution mechanism works for args and also for $(find package_name) which resolves package directories. A common error is forgetting to provide a needed arg at launch time when there's no default; roslaunch will report a missing argument. Troubleshooting launch files is a vital skill. Common errors include "Cannot find package" when the package is not in ROS_PACKAGE_PATH — the fix is to source your workspace's setup. bash so roslaunch can locate packages. "Cannot find executable" often means the type attribute points to a non-existing file or a Python script lacks the executable bit; fix with chmod +x and verify the file name. "Permission denied" similarly indicates missing execute permissions. If a node dies immediately, use output="screen" to see its stack trace and correct runtime errors. "Topic not found" usually stems from incorrect remap rules or a publisher not starting; check rostopic list and ensure namespaces and leading slashes are correct. Use rosnode list to verify which nodes are running and rosparam get/list to inspect parameter values. When a node is marked required="true" it will cause the entire launch to shut down if it exits — this is useful for safety but can cause unexpected full shutdowns during debugging. Methodical checks of paths, permissions, and output logs will quickly reveal the root cause. Troubleshooting launch files means check package paths, executable permissions, node output, and parameter/topic lists; output="screen" and rosnode/rosparam tools are your first tools.. Keep these three ideas in mind as you work with launch files. First, launch files are XML configuration that both configures and starts your ROS system, making multi-node runs reproducible.
